cap: Three male-tract questions each end in one structure. Urethral folds that fail to fuse leave a ventral opening, hypospadias; a genital tubercle formed in the wrong place gives a dorsal opening, epispadias, with bladder exstrophy. The testis follows the gubernaculum through the abdominal wall and takes a covering from each layer, so the internal oblique gives the cremaster. Undescended testes keep a raised germ cell tumor risk.
teach: Descent has two phases. In the transabdominal phase INSL3 from Leydig cells swells the gubernaculum and holds the testis near the deep inguinal ring, an opening in the transversalis fascia lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. In the inguinoscrotal phase, which depends on androgen and falls mostly in the last trimester, the testis passes through the canal into the scrotum; the processus vaginalis precedes it, its proximal part then obliterates, and the distal part remains as the tunica vaginalis. Failed descent matters for three reasons: the warm abdominal or canal position impairs sperm production, germ cell tumor risk rises and persists in both testes even after orchiopexy, and the open processus vaginalis that often accompanies it allows hernia or hydrocele. Early orchiopexy improves fertility and makes the testis easy to examine, but it does not remove the cancer risk.
